title: Human training data: how it gets made, from screening test to rubric
summary: Ada and Alan teach how human training data is made: InstructGPT's demonstrations, rankings and labeler screening, Llama 2's shift from writing to weekly preference judging, expert-written rubrics (HealthBench, Rubrics as Rewards) and what experts are paid, the supply chain from Sama's Kenyan labelers to the Meta-Scale neutrality fallout, and how honest labels still teach sycophancy or turn out not to be human.

topics: deep dive: human training data — how it gets made
concepts_taught: human training data as three products: demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning, rankings/comparisons that train a reward model, and prompt-only sets for the RL stage (InstructGPT: ~40 contractors via Upwork and Scale AI; ~13k/33k/31k prompts; K=4-9 rankings)

labeler selection and whose preferences get learned: InstructGPT's four-part screening test with soft 75% agreement cutoffs, ~73% inter-labeler agreement, most comparisons labeled once for cost, and alignment to labelers, researchers (instructions) and API customers

the shift from writing to judging: Llama 2 stopped SFT at 27,540 vendor annotations once model outputs rivaled them, then bought ~1.4M graded binary comparisons in weekly batches to keep the reward model on-distribution; vendors yielding markedly different models

expert rubrics as reusable judgment: HealthBench's 262 physicians and 48,562 weighted criteria applied by a validated model grader, and Rubrics as Rewards turning reference-answer rubrics into RL reward; expert pay and its impermanence

how honest human labels teach the wrong thing: agreement with the user's views predicts preference (Sharma et al.), preference models favoring convincing sycophancy, and crowd workers using LLMs (33-46%), plus vendor neutrality after Meta's Scale stake
